mainTopic: Checks during the seven clean days of a זב or זבה, and the immersions of a confused woman (טועה)
overview: A זב or זבה must count seven clean days (שבעה נקיים) before becoming טהור. The גמרא first asks about someone who checked only on day one and day eight. רב says that for רבי אליעזר the day-one check alone is enough. רבי חנינא says a check is needed at both ends of the seven days. A ברייתא saying 'they agree' that only day eight counts is answered: the Sages who agree are רבי יהושע and רבי עקיבא. Next, רב rules about a זבה who stopped bleeding on her third day. After a challenge from רב ששת, the ruling is explained: even if she checks only on the seventh day, that end check makes the seven days count. This is the mirror image of his first ruling. An objection from a טועה, a confused woman who immerses only at night, is pushed aside because that ruling follows רבי עקיבא, who requires the days to be counted before us. The גמרא then quotes a ברייתא about a טועה who immerses 9, 11 or 15 times. רבא mocks the 15 with the story of the unfair town גלחי. The ברייתא is re-read, and the breakdown of the fifteen immersions begins, continuing on the next amud.

steps.title: What does רבי אליעזר hold about checking on day one and day eight?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבי אליעזר needs a check at both the start and the end of the seven days, or whether a check at the start alone is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי אליעזר, what is the law? Do we need a check at both the beginning and the end of the seven days? If so, here there is a check at the beginning but none at the end. Or maybe a check at the beginning is enough, even with no check at the end?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the case of a זב or זבה who checked themselves on day one and day eight. It asks how רבי אליעזר would rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר already said that checking on day one and day seven makes all seven days count. Here the second check came on day eight, which is outside the seven. So the question is: what made the seven days count for רבי אליעזר? Was it the check on day one alone, or a check on both edges of the seven?

keyTerms.meaning: Their beginning: here, a check on the first of the seven days
Their end: here, a check on the last (seventh) day
We need / we require
Or perhaps: introduces the second side of a question
The seven clean days a זב or זבה must count before becoming טהור

steps.confusionAlert: Day eight is not part of the seven days. The question is not whether day eight counts. It is whether days one through seven count when there was no check on day seven itself.

phrases.english: According to Rabbi Eliezer, what is the law?
Do we require their beginning and their end,
and here there is their beginning but not their end,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִילְמָא תְּחִלָּתָן אַף עַל גַּב שֶׁאֵין סוֹפָן?
phrases.english: or perhaps their beginning is enough, even though there is not their end?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the case of checking on the first and eighth days, raised just before this point on the daf.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבי אליעזר's rule depends on a check on day one alone, or on checks on both day one and day seven.

steps.title: רב: the first-day check alone is enough
steps.stepSummary: רב says this case is the same as checking on day one and day seven. The check on day one is enough even without a check at the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: This case is the same as that one. The check at the beginning is enough, even though there is no check at the end.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question. For רבי אליעזר, checking on day one and day eight works just like checking on day one and day seven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, what counts for רבי אליעזר is the clean check on day one. That check sets up a presumption that the following days are clean as well. So all seven days count, and day eight is extra.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the same as that: the two cases are identical
Even though

phrases.english: Rav said: This is the same as that. Their beginning is enough,
phrases.notes: 'This is that' means checking on days one and eight is treated just like checking on days one and seven.

phrases.english: even though there is not their end.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1 by choosing its second side.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: For רבי אליעזר, a clean check on day one alone is enough to count all seven days.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: both a first-day and a last-day check are needed
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא says רבי אליעזר requires a check at both the start and the end of the seven days. Here there was no check on day seven, so the days do not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: We need a check at both the beginning and the end. Here there is a check at the beginning but not at the end.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא disagrees with רב and chooses the first side of the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי חנינא, רבי אליעזר lets the middle days count only because clean checks surround them on both sides. A check on day eight does not close off the seven days. So in this case the first seven days are not counted.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: in this case
There is / there is not

steps.whatToRemember: רב says the day-one check alone is enough. רבי חנינא says a check is needed at both ends of the seven days.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Chanina said:
We require their beginning and their end,
and here there is their beginning, but not their end.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite answer to רב's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: For רבי אליעזר, checks on both the first and the last of the seven days are needed. Without the day-seven check, the days do not count.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to show רבי אליעזר agrees only day eight counts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: 'they agree' that a זב or זבה who checked on day one and day eight gets only day eight. It suggests the ones who agree are רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע, which would go against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא raises an objection: They agree about a זב and a זבה who checked themselves on the first day and the eighth day and found themselves clean: they have only the eighth day. Who are the ones who agree? Is it not רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב with a ברייתא. It assumes the Sages who 'agree' include רבי אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'agree' suggests Sages who disagree elsewhere and agree here. רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע disagree about checking on day one and day seven. If they agree that checking on day one and day eight gives only day eight, then רבי אליעזר does not count the first seven days, and רב is wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: And they agree: Sages who disagree elsewhere agree in this case
A man or woman who had a discharge that makes them טמא and requires seven clean days
Checked themselves: an examination to confirm they are clean
Is it not?: introduces a suggested reading

phrases.english: They raised an objection: And they agree about a zav and a zava

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבָּדְקוּ עַצְמָן יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן וְיוֹם שְׁמִינִי
phrases.english: who examined themselves on the first day and the eighth day
and found themselves pure,
that they have only the eighth day alone.
phrases.notes: Only day eight counts toward the seven clean days. The first seven days are not counted.

phrases.english: Who are the ones who agree?
Is it not Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב's position from step 2 using a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's view that, for רבי אליעזר, the day-one check alone makes all seven days count.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'they agree' means רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע, then רבי אליעזר holds that only day eight counts. That directly contradicts רב.

steps.title: The ones who agree are רבי יהושע and רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the 'agreeing' Sages are רבי יהושע and רבי עקיבא, not רבי אליעזר. רב's view stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It is רבי יהושע and רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב. It says the ברייתא is about a different pair of Sages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע and רבי עקיבא also disagree about the day-one and day-seven case, so 'they agree' can refer to them. Both of them hold that only day eight counts here. רבי אליעזר is left out, so he can still hold like רב that the clean check on day one makes days one through seven count.

keyTerms.meaning: No: rejects the suggested reading
A presumption of cleanness: here, the status set by a clean check on day one

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא does not refute רב, because the Sages who 'agree' are רבי יהושע and רבי עקיבא. רבי אליעזר may still hold that the day-one check alone is enough.

phrases.english: No, it is Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the identification of the 'agreeing' Sages in step 4 and so protects רב.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reidentifying who the ברייתא is talking about
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'They agree' meant רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע, so רבי אליעזר would count only day eight.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'They agree' means רבי יהושע and רבי עקיבא. רבי אליעזר is not included, so רב's reading of him still stands.

steps.title: רב's ruling about stopping on the third day
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a woman who stopped bleeding in purity on her third day counts toward her seven clean days.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said in the name of רב ירמיה בר אבא, in the name of רב: A נדה who did the check showing she had moved into purity on her third day counts it toward the seven clean days.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling of רב, passed down through two students, about when the count of seven clean days begins. This opens a new short discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The woman saw blood, and on her third day she checked and found herself clean. רב says this counts toward the seven clean days. The next steps will ask what exactly this means and which woman it is talking about.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman who is impure because of her regular monthly bleeding
She did a check showing she had stopped bleeding and was moving toward purity
Seven clean days, with no bleeding, that some women must count before purity

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said
that Rav Yirmeya bar Abba said
that Rav said:
A menstruating woman who checked and found herself pure
on her third day
counts it toward the number of seven clean days.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת, אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא, אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new statement of רב about counting clean days, related to the earlier topic of checks during the seven days.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman who checked and found herself pure on her third day counts toward the seven clean days.

steps.title: Why would a נדה need to count?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that a נדה does not count clean days at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: A נדה, why does she need counting?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of רב's ruling. A נדה does not count seven clean days, so the word נדה cannot be right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נדה's seven days are simply seven days from when the bleeding started. She does not need them to be clean days. Only a זבה must count seven clean days, so talking about 'counting' for a נדה makes no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: Counting, here meaning counting the seven clean days

phrases.english: A menstruating woman, why does she need counting?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of רב's ruling in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word נדה in רב's ruling
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A נדה does not count seven clean days, so a ruling about her counting cannot be talking about a נדה.

steps.title: Read it as a זבה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the ruling to be about a זבה, who does count seven clean days.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: A זבה who did the check showing she had moved into purity on her third day counts it toward the seven clean days.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem by changing one word: the ruling is about a זבה, not a נדה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A זבה, who saw blood for three days outside her regular time, must count seven clean days. So now the ruling makes sense. The rest of the ruling stays exactly the same.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say: the גמרא changes the wording of a statement
A woman who saw blood for several days outside her regular time and must count seven clean days

phrases.english: Rather, say:
A zava who checked and found herself pure
on her third day
counts it toward the number of seven clean days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7 by changing נדה to זבה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ruling was about a נדה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ruling is about a זבה, who really does count seven clean days.

steps.title: Does רב follow the כותאי?
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת asks if רב is following the כותאי, who count the day of stopping as one of the seven.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said to רב ירמיה בר אבא: Did רב say his teaching like the כותאי? They say that the day she stops counts toward the seven!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת challenges the ruling itself. It sounds like the view of the כותאי, which is not accepted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling sounds like the third day, the day she stopped, is itself one of the seven clean days. That is exactly what the כותאי say. Our הלכה requires seven full clean days after the day she stops, so רב cannot mean this.

keyTerms.meaning: The Samaritans, a group whose rulings the Sages did not accept
Stops, meaning stops seeing blood
A teaching or ruling

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת לְרַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said to Rav Yirmeya bar Abba:
Did Rav say his teaching like the Samaritans?
For they say: the day on which she stops
counts toward the number of seven!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת לְרַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא: רַב כְּכוּתָאֵי אַמְרַהּ לִשְׁמַעְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the ruling is about a זבה, רב ששת challenges what it actually says.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the third day counts toward the seven
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Counting the day of stopping as one of the seven is the view of the כותאי, which the Sages reject.

steps.title: רב meant: not counting the third day
steps.stepSummary: רב ירמיה בר אבא explains that רב meant the count starts after the third day.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב said it, he meant apart from the third day.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ירמיה בר אבא answers that רב did not mean the third day itself counts. The seven days start after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'counts it' are now read differently. The check on the third day lets her begin counting, but the third day itself is not one of the seven. This removes the problem of the כותאי.

keyTerms.meaning: Apart from, not including

phrases.english: When Rav said it, he meant apart from the third day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ששת's challenge in step 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The third day itself counts as one of the seven, like the כותאי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The count of seven begins after the third day.

steps.title: Then it is obvious
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת objects that if the count simply starts after day three, רב is saying nothing new.
steps.simpleTranslation: Apart from the third day? That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת pushes back. If רב only meant the count starts after the third day, why would he need to say it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone knows a זבה counts seven clean days after she stops. So the new reading makes רב's ruling seem pointless. The גמרא now needs to show what new point רב is teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious, so why say it?

phrases.english: Apart from the third day? That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the count starts after the third day
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that is all רב meant, his ruling teaches nothing new.

steps.title: The new point: no check until the seventh day
steps.stepSummary: The ruling teaches that the days count even if she did not check again until the seventh day.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where she did not check again until the seventh day.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer explains what is new in רב's ruling. She checked on the third day and then did not check again until the seventh day, and the days still count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the check on the day she stopped, she did not check again until the seventh day, so there was no check on the first of the seven days. Still, all seven days count, because of the check at the end. The next step spells this out: this is the reverse of רב's ruling in step 2, where a check at the start alone was enough.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed: the גמרא shows a case where the ruling teaches something new
She checked herself

steps.whatToRemember: רב's ruling is about a זבה. The day she stops is not one of the seven. If she then checks only on the seventh day, that end check is enough for all seven days to count.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the third day itself counts as a clean day. That is the view of the כותאי. Here the check on the third day only opens the count that starts afterward.
steps.whyThisMatters: This adds a second rule to רב's view in the earlier debate with רבי חנינא. Earlier, a check at the start alone was enough. Here, a check at the end alone is enough.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for a case where she did not check until the seventh day.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, כְּגוֹן דְּלֹא בָּדְקָה עַד שְׁבִיעִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of step 11 by giving a case with a real new point.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing to a case where the ruling teaches something new
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's ruling only says the count starts after the third day, which is obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב teaches that her check on the third day makes the days count even with no checks until the seventh day.

steps.title: רב taught two mirror-image rulings
steps.stepSummary: רב taught two things. Earlier, a check at the beginning is enough without one at the end. Here, a check at the end is enough without one at the beginning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Over there רב taught us that a check at the beginning of the days counts even without a check at the end. Here he teaches us that a check at the end counts even without a check at the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer to רב ששת. It shows that רב's ruling here is not a repeat, because it is the opposite side of what he taught earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת had complained that רב was saying nothing new. The answer is that רב's earlier ruling covered a check only at the start. This ruling covers a check only at the end, so each one teaches something the other does not.

keyTerms.meaning: their beginning (a check at the start of the seven days)
their end (a check at the end of the seven days)
even though there is not
he is teaching us (something new)

phrases.english: And he taught us there:
phrases.notes: "There" means רב's earlier ruling, said about רבי אליעזר's view.

phrases.aramaic: תְּחִלָּתָן, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין סוֹפָן,
phrases.english: a check at their beginning works, even though there is none at their end,
and here he teaches us:

phrases.aramaic: סוֹפָן, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין תְּחִלָּתָן.
phrases.english: a check at their end works, even though there is none at their beginning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer from Step 12 by setting it side by side with רב's earlier ruling.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the ruling is new because it covers the reverse case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's ruling here just repeats his earlier one.
steps.terutzMaskana: The two rulings are mirror images: a beginning check alone, and an end check alone.

steps.title: Why the second ruling was needed
steps.stepSummary: Without this ruling, we might think only a beginning check works, because it sets up a חזקה of being clean. So רב had to tell us that an end check alone also works.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that a check at the beginning without one at the end is what we accept, because we keep the days in their established clean status. But a check at the end without one at the beginning would not work. So רב teaches us that it does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why we could not have figured out the second ruling on our own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A check at the beginning creates a חזקה: we saw she was clean, so we assume she stayed clean. A check only at the end has no such starting point, so we might have rejected it. רב tells us it still counts.

keyTerms.meaning: you might have said (introduces a mistaken assumption)
we keep them in their established status (חזקה)
a presumed status that stays until shown otherwise

steps.whatToRemember: A check at the beginning alone is enough, and a check at the end alone is also enough, even though only the beginning check sets up a חזקה.

phrases.english: For you might have said:

phrases.aramaic: תְּחִלָּתָן אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין סוֹפָן
phrases.english: a check at their beginning, even though there is none at their end,
is what we accept,
since we keep the days in their established status,
phrases.notes: Once she checked and was clean, we assume she stayed clean.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל סוֹפָן אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין תְּחִלָּתָן — לָא,
phrases.english: but a check at their end, even though there is none at their beginning, would not work,
so he teaches us that it does.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the second ruling in Step 13 was needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the need for both rulings (צריכותא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only a beginning check works, because it sets up a חזקה.
steps.terutzMaskana: An end check alone also works, even with no חזקה from the start.

steps.title: Is that really so? רבין's report about a טועה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the ruling. It brings רבין's report that רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא raised an objection from the case of a טועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But when רבין came, he said: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא raised an objection from the case of a טועה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a challenge to what was just said. It is setting up the next move by bringing in a report from רבין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "אִינִי" signals doubt about the conclusion that an end check alone is enough. The challenge is built from a case discussed elsewhere: a טועה, a woman unsure of her status. The full point of the challenge comes in the next lines.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? (signals a challenge)
a woman who is unsure of her status

phrases.english: Is that so?
But when רבין came, he said:
רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא raised an objection from the case of a "טועה".
phrases.notes: This refers to a case discussed earlier in the מסכת, on 29a.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָא כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of Steps 13–14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the clean days count with only a check at the end
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A report about the טועה is brought, which seems to show a different approach to counting clean days.

steps.title: רבין: a טועה immerses only at night in her first week
steps.stepSummary: רבין says he cannot see the force of the objection. We already hold that in the first week she comes before us, she immerses at night but not by day.
steps.simpleTranslation: And I do not know what his objection is. For we hold: in the first week that she comes before us, we have her immerse at night, but we do not have her immerse by day.
steps.whatsHappening: רבין continues his report and states an accepted rule about the טועה. The גמרא is setting up the challenge to our sugya through this rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבין says the objection is weak because of a known rule: in her first week, a טועה immerses only at night, never by day. The rule matters here because a daytime immersion would only make sense once seven clean days were counted.

keyTerms.meaning: a strong refutation or objection
we hold as an established rule
the first week
we have her immerse (in a מקוה)
nights / daytime

steps.title: Why not let her immerse by day too?
steps.stepSummary: If days did not have to be counted before us, the woman should also immerse by day, since she might have finished her counting already. Because she does not, it seems we require counting before us, which goes against רב.

steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the full force of the objection from step 15. The rule that she immerses only at night seems to prove that her clean days must be counted in front of us.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Immersing by day only makes sense if her seven clean days might already be done. The ruling refuses a daytime immersion, so it seems days she counted on her own do not count. That clashes with רב, who counted days even when there was only a check at the end.

steps.title: The confused woman who saw one day: nine immersions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a confused woman who saw blood on one day. She immerses nine times: seven for נדה and two for זיבה.

steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts its proof by quoting a ברייתא about a woman who doesn't know whether she is in her נדה days or her זיבה days. The proof itself will be finished in the coming lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She doesn't know which kind of days she is in, so she must immerse in a way that covers both. Seven immersions cover the chance that the blood was נדה. Two more cover the chance that it was זיבה.

steps.title: If she saw at twilight: eleven immersions
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. If the confused woman saw blood at twilight, she must immerse eleven times.

steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second case. When the blood was seen at twilight, the number of immersions goes up from nine to eleven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Twilight is a time when we are unsure whether it is still day or already night. That added doubt raises the count. The גמרא will work out the exact count next.

keyTerms.meaning: Twilight, a time of doubt whether it is still day or already night
Eleven

phrases.english: "I saw impure blood at twilight":
we have her immerse eleven immersions.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A confused woman who saw blood at twilight immerses eleven times.

steps.title: Why eleven immersions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the eleven immersions in the ברייתא are for.
steps.simpleTranslation: The eleven immersions: what are they for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a woman who saw blood at בין השמשות needs eleven immersions instead of the nine mentioned before. This question sets up רב ירמיה מדפתי's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the regular case she needed nine: seven for נדה and two for זיבה. The ברייתא jumps to eleven for twilight, so the גמרא wants to know where the extra two come from.

steps.title: She came to us at twilight: eight for נדה and three for זיבה
steps.stepSummary: רב ירמיה מדפתי explains that she came before the court at twilight, so she needs eight immersions for נדה and three for זיבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ירמיה מדפתי said: For example, she came before us at twilight. So there are eight immersions for נדה and three for זיבה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ירמיה מדפתי answers the question. The case is a woman who arrived at בין השמשות, and that adds one immersion for נדה and one for זיבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בין השמשות might be day or might already be night, so we cannot be sure which day her bleeding belongs to. Because of that doubt, the count can shift by a day. This adds one more night immersion for נדה (eight instead of seven) and one more day immersion for זיבה (three instead of two).

steps.deeperAnalysis: This is surprising. A woman who saw no blood gets more immersions than a woman who did see blood, who needed only nine or eleven. That oddity sets up רבא's sharp criticism in the next step.

steps.title: רבא: this law is like the twisted laws of גלחי
steps.stepSummary: רבא criticizes the fifteen-immersion ruling as illogical, comparing it to the unfair law of the town גלחי, where a man without an ox had to shepherd longer than a man with one.

steps.deeperAnalysis: In גלחי, the man with no ox, who gains nothing from the herd, had to work twice as hard. In the same way, the woman who saw no blood ends up with more immersions than the woman who did. רבא's point is that the result is upside down.

steps.title: The orphan slaughters the oxen and divides the skins

steps.deeperAnalysis: The orphan, who owned no ox, had to shepherd extra under the town's law. He turns their rule back on them: the person with no ox gets more skins. The story makes fun of the twisted logic רבא criticized.

steps.title: The townspeople ask: what are you saying?
steps.stepSummary: The people of גלחי ask the orphan to explain his strange division.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: What is this that you are saying?
steps.whatsHappening: The townspeople protest and ask the orphan for his reasoning. This sets up his clever reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the townspeople feel the unfairness when it works against them. Their question opens the door for the orphan to point out that this is their own logic.

keyTerms.meaning: What is this that you are saying?

phrases.english: They said to him: What is this that you are saying?

steps.title: The end of the law follows the beginning of the law
steps.stepSummary: The orphan answers that the end of the law should match the beginning: if the one with no ox was 'preferred' for shepherding, he is also preferred for the skins.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: The end of the law is like the beginning of the law. At the beginning of the law, wasn't the one who has no ox preferred? At the end of the law too, the one who has no ox is preferred.
steps.whatsHappening: The orphan explains himself. Since the town gave the no-ox man the bigger share of work, he now gets the bigger share of skins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He uses the town's own rule against them. If 'no ox' means 'more' when it comes to work, then 'no ox' should also mean 'more' when it comes to reward. The story drives home רבא's point that the fifteen-immersion law is backwards.

steps.title: Applying the parable: less blood cannot require more immersions
steps.stepSummary: רבא applies the lesson of גלחי to the ברייתא. If a woman who says 'I saw' needs only nine or eleven טבילות, how can a woman who says 'I did not see' need fifteen?
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too: if a woman who says 'I saw blood' needs only nine or eleven immersions, can it be that a woman who says 'I saw no blood' needs fifteen?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now ties the גלחי story back to רבא's criticism of the ברייתא. It shows that the ruling has the same backwards logic as that town's law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In גלחי, the man with less (no ox) got the heavier burden. Here the woman with 'less' (no blood at all) gets the heavier burden of fifteen טבילות. The woman who actually saw blood gets only nine or eleven, which seems upside down.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too: the same idea applies in this case

steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a woman who says she saw no blood needs fifteen טבילות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A woman with no reported blood should not need more טבילות than a woman who did see blood. Giving her more is as backwards as the law of גלחי.

steps.title: Re-reading the ברייתא: she saw but does not know when
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-reads the ברייתא. The fifteen-immersion case is a woman who saw blood but doesn't know how much, or whether it was in ימי נדה or ימי זיבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, read the ברייתא like this: if she says 'I saw blood, but I don't know how much I saw, or whether I saw it in the days of נדה or the days of זיבה,' then we have her immerse fifteen times.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רבא by changing how we read the ברייתא. The fifteen-immersion woman is not someone who saw nothing. She saw blood and is confused about the details.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the case sounded like 'I saw nothing,' which made fifteen טבילות seem unfair. Now the case is double confusion: unknown amount and unknown timing (נדה or זיבה). That extra doubt is what calls for more טבילות, so the backwards logic disappears.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say it like this: the גמרא re-reads a source

steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to explain the fifteen. If she comes to us during the day, we first give her seven טבילות for נדה.

steps.deeperAnalysis: Since she might have seen during ימי נדה, she needs seven טבילות to cover the possibility of נדה. The timing detail, coming during the day, matters for how the count is set up. The rest of the fifteen will be explained next.
